extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory textbook chapter analyzing the role of language, names, and propositions in logic and setting methodological limits on logical analysis; explains classifications of names and the structure of propositions with examples and practical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic defined as science of operations for estimating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the science of the operations of the understanding which are subservient to the estimation of evidence: both the process itself of advancing from known truths to unknown, and all other intellectual operations in so far as auxiliary to this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the process of reasoning/inference and any mental operations instrumental to assessing evidence; logic's scope is determined by what is necessary for practical ends (the art of reasoning). It bears on metaphysics only insofar as that discipline draws inferences from evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Naming, Definition, and Classification within logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic includes the operation of Naming; it includes, also, Definition, and Classification, because these operations marshal facts and make evidence and conclusions permanent and accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language is an instrument of thought; correct use of names and classifications helps perceive evidence more clearly and reduces errors. These operations are treated as specially instrumental to the estimation of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit analytic depth to what is necessary for practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not decompose mental operations into ultimate elements beyond the point required for distinguishing correct from incorrect performances; analysis should go only so far as is requisite for practical logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: one need not know muscle anatomy to learn exercises, except where a defect matters. Overly deep metaphysical decomposition is unnecessary for logical practice. The point at which inaccuracies become visible is the practical stopping point for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin logic with analysis of language
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry into language (the meaning and right use of words) is a necessary preliminary to the study of logic because reasoning usually occurs by means of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those without a thorough insight into the signification and purposes of words are likely to reason incorrectly. Teaching the meaning and use of terms first removes a major source of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze propositions as composed of Subject, Predicate, and Copula
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is discourse in which something is affirmed or denied of something; every proposition consists of three parts: the Subject, the Predicate, and the Copula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Gold is yellow' (predicate = yellow, subject = gold, copula = is). Understanding this structure is the first step to analyzing the objects of belief and the kinds of questions that can be framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim/belief requires two names (objects) combined
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest act of belief supposes two objects (two names): one object is not sufficient; belief involves bringing one name under another (subject and predicate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The sun exists' combines 'the sun' and 'existence' — without the second element there is no proposition to believe. This shows that propositions necessarily involve relation between distinct items of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat names as names of things (not merely ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names should be regarded as the names of the things themselves (what we intend to be understood when we use them), not merely as names of our ideas of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes's view that names are signs of conceptions is noted, but the text argues we use names to assert beliefs about things (e.g., 'the sun is the cause of day' refers to a physical fact, not merely to ideas). Use words as names of their referents in predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish words that are not names (syncategorematic) from names (categorematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words (particles like 'of', 'to', inflected cases, and some adjectives in contexts) are not names by themselves and cannot be used as the subject of a proposition except when speaking of the word itself; such are called syncategorematic terms, while words usable alone as subject or predicate are categorematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'of', 'to', 'me', 'him' are not names unless referring to the word itself. Adjectives can function as names in predicates ('snow is white') or even as subjects by ellipsis ('White is an agreeable color'), but this is grammatical convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-worded expressions can form a single name (categorematic term)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of words often composes one single name (a many-worded categorematic term) when, by predication, they yield a single assertion rather than several.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by predication: 'John Nokes, who was the mayor of the town, died yesterday' counts as one name; by contrast, 'John Nokes and the mayor of the town died yesterday' makes two assertions hence two names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general names from individual (singular) names
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is capable of being truly affirmed, in the same sense, of each of an indefinite number of things; an individual or singular name is capable of being truly affirmed of only one thing (in the same sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'man' is general (applies alike to many individuals); 'John' is individual. 'The king who succeeded William the Conqueror' is an individual name. Avoid defining 'general' merely as 'name of a class'—prefer treating 'class' as derivative from general names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general names from collective names
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name can be predicated of each individual of a multitude; a collective name cannot be predicated of each separately but only of the whole taken together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the 76th regiment' is a collective (not general) name: it cannot be predicated of individual soldiers; 'a regiment' is both collective and general (general across different regiments but collective with respect to soldiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish concrete names from abstract names
rubrics_metrics.description: A concrete name stands for a thing (object); an abstract name stands for an attribute of a thing (quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'John', 'the sea', 'this table' are concrete; 'whiteness' is abstract (name of a quality). The author adheres to the older scholastic distinction (concrete = objects, abstract = attributes) and warns against the modern misuse of 'abstract' to mean any general name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that some abstract names are general and some are neither
rubrics_metrics.description: Some abstract names (like 'color' or 'magnitude') denote a class of attributes and are general; others that denote a single attribute (like 'visibleness', 'equality') are neither clearly general nor individual and may merit separate treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating 'abstract' with 'general'; treat names like 'whiteness' or 'visibleness' carefully—some abstract terms apply to many instances (general), while others denote a single attribute (neither general nor individual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat adjectives and their related abstract nouns according to principal use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a word is taken as name of an attribute or as name of objects depends on how it is principally used in predication: 'white' is used as a name of white objects, while 'whiteness' is the name of the quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When we say 'snow is white' we do not mean snow is a color; we mean snow has the color. Thus distinguish usage-based signification: the adjective implies the attribute but is a name of objects possessing it, whereas the abstract noun names the attribute itself.
